name: Hydrogen meets oxygen
energy: gives off heat (needs a spark to start)
dH: about −286 kJ per mole of hydrogen
story: A spark shakes things hard. Each hydrogen pair (H2) lets go of its one handshake, and each oxygen pair (O2) lets go of its double handshake.
Now the atoms float loose: each hydrogen has 1 empty hand, and each oxygen has 2.
Each oxygen grabs two hydrogens, one in each hand. That's water (H2O).
The new grips are tighter than the old ones, like a spring snapping shut, so energy comes out as heat. That heat shakes the next molecules apart, which is why the fire keeps itself going.
everyday: A hydrogen fuel cell does this same swap slowly and turns the energy into electricity instead of a flame. The only exhaust is water.

lens.rocket: The Space Shuttle main engines burned liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen. The exhaust was mostly hot steam.

intro: Hydrogen burning in oxygen. The only thing it makes is water, plus a burst of heat. Rocket engines and hydrogen fuel cells run on this.
takeaway: Burning means breaking weaker grips and making tighter ones. The difference comes out as heat.

name: Hydrogen meets chlorine
energy: gives off heat (a spark or strong light starts it)
dH: about −92 kJ per mole of HCl
story: Light or a spark snaps the chlorine pair (Cl2) apart first. Its single handshake is the weakest grip here.
A loose chlorine has 1 empty hand. It steals a hydrogen out of a hydrogen pair (H2), and the other hydrogen is left alone with an empty hand.
That lonely hydrogen steals a chlorine from the next pair. Each steal frees a new atom, like falling dominoes. Chemists call this a chain reaction.
When it settles, every hydrogen holds one chlorine (HCl). Those grips are tighter than the old ones, so heat comes out.
everyday: Burning hydrogen in chlorine is one way factories make hydrogen chloride. Dissolved in water, it becomes hydrochloric acid, used to clean steel and in many other jobs.
intro: Hydrogen gas meets chlorine gas, and they make hydrogen chloride. Dissolved in water, that's hydrochloric acid, which is used to clean steel.
takeaway: One loose atom can set off a whole chain of swaps. That's why this mix can go off with a bang.

name: Sodium meets chlorine
dH: about −411 kJ per mole of salt
story: The chlorine pair (Cl2) lets go of its handshake, so each chlorine is on its own.
Each sodium has 1 loose outer electron. Giving it away is far easier than finding 7 more, so sodium gives.
Sodium hands its electron to a chlorine. Sodium is now positive (Na+, missing an electron), and chlorine is negative (Cl−, one extra). Nothing is shared. This is a handoff, not a handshake.
Plus and minus pull together like magnets. Billions of them stack into tiny cubes, and that's salt. Settling into the stack releases heat.
everyday: The salt on your table is mined or dried from seawater, not made this way. But the demo shows why salt is so stable: both atoms got what they wanted.
intro: Sodium, a soft shiny metal, meets chlorine, a poisonous green gas. Together they make table salt. Two dangerous things make a safe one, because each atom gets exactly what it wants.
takeaway: Metals give electrons, and nonmetals take them. The + and − then stick like magnets. That's called an ionic bond.

name: Peroxide fizzing
dH: about −98 kJ per mole of peroxide
story: In peroxide (H2O2), two oxygens hold each other with a weak grip. It snaps easily, and even faster with a helper, like an enzyme in your blood (a natural helper molecule).
After the snap, each oxygen still holds one hydrogen and has one empty hand.
Hydrogens get passed around until two oxygens each hold two hydrogens. Those are water molecules (H2O).
The two leftover oxygens grab each other with a double handshake. That's oxygen gas (O2): the bubbles. Everything ends up more settled, so a little heat comes out.
everyday: Pour peroxide on a cut and it foams. An enzyme in your blood called catalase speeds up this exact reaction.

lens.rocket: The German V-2 used concentrated hydrogen peroxide, broken down this way, to make hot steam that spun its fuel pumps.

intro: Hydrogen peroxide, the brown-bottle stuff for cuts, falls apart into water and oxygen gas. The foam you see on a cut is oxygen bubbles.
takeaway: A weak bond breaks, the atoms trade partners, and the gas that escapes is the fizz.

name: Burning natural gas
energy: gives off heat (needs a flame or spark to start)
dH: about −890 kJ per mole of methane
story: The flame shakes everything hard. Methane's carbon lets go of its 4 hydrogens, and each oxygen pair (O2) lets go of its double handshake.
Carbon now has 4 empty hands. It grabs 2 oxygens and holds each one with 2 hands. That's carbon dioxide (CO2).
The 4 loose hydrogens pair up with the other 2 oxygens, 2 hydrogens per oxygen. That's 2 waters (H2O).
The new grips are much tighter than the old ones, like springs snapping shut. The extra energy comes out as heat and light, which keeps the flame going.
everyday: This is your gas stove, furnace, or water heater. Natural gas is mostly methane.

lens.rocket: Starship's Raptor engines burn methane with liquid oxygen. This is the same reaction, run at very high pressure.

intro: Natural gas burning, like on a gas stove. Methane plus oxygen from the air turns into carbon dioxide and water vapor, plus a lot of heat.
takeaway: Every atom you started with is still here. They just swapped partners, and the tighter grips released heat.

name: Iron rusting
dH: about −824 kJ per mole of Fe2O3
story: Oxygen floats around in pairs (O2), held by a double handshake. First the pairs split, so each oxygen is on its own and wants 2 more electrons.
Iron is a metal, so it doesn't share. It gives electrons away. Here each iron gives 3.
4 irons give 12 electrons. 6 oxygens take 2 each, which is also 12, so every electron has a new home. Iron is now positive (+3) and oxygen is negative (−2).
Plus and minus stick together like magnets into a reddish solid: rust (Fe2O3). Heat comes out, but so slowly you never feel it.
everyday: Rust on cars, nails, and bridges. Real rust also needs water, and salt speeds it up. This shows only the iron and oxygen part. Hand warmer packets use fast rusting iron to make heat.

lens.rocket: Starship is built from stainless steel. Its chromium forms a very thin oxide skin that seals the surface and keeps rust from spreading.

intro: Iron slowly combining with oxygen from the air. The reddish-brown flaky stuff is rust. It's the same kind of reaction as burning, just very slow.
takeaway: Rusting is slow burning. Iron gives electrons, oxygen takes them, and the + and − clump together into rust.

name: Burning alcohol
energy: gives off heat (needs a flame to start)
dH: about −1,367 kJ per mole of ethanol
story: The flame shakes ethanol apart, and every grip lets go. The oxygen pairs (O2) from the air split too.
Ethanol already carries 1 oxygen of its own, so it needs a bit less oxygen from the air than a fuel without one.
Each of the 2 carbons grabs 2 oxygens and holds each with 2 hands. That's 2 carbon dioxides (CO2).
The 6 hydrogens pair up with 3 oxygens to make 3 waters (H2O). The new grips are tighter, so heat pours out.
everyday: Alcohol burners, fondue pots, and the ethanol blended into most US gasoline.

lens.rocket: The German V-2 burned an ethanol and water mix with liquid oxygen. The water helped keep the engine cooler.

intro: Alcohol (ethanol) burning, like in a fondue burner. It turns into carbon dioxide and water, the same leftovers as burning natural gas.
takeaway: Fuels made of carbon and hydrogen all burn the same way, into carbon dioxide and water, plus heat.

name: Adding hydrogen
energy: gives off heat (needs a metal catalyst to get going)
dH: about −137 kJ per mole of ethylene
story: Ethylene's two carbons hold each other with a double handshake. The second handshake is the weaker one.
A metal surface like nickel helps. It's a catalyst: a helper that speeds a reaction up without getting used up. It pulls the hydrogen pair (H2) apart.
The second carbon-to-carbon handshake lets go. Now each carbon has 1 empty hand.
Each carbon grabs one hydrogen, so every hand now holds a single grip. That's ethane. It's more settled, so heat comes out.
everyday: Food makers add hydrogen to vegetable oils this same way to make them more solid, as in margarine.

lens.nexus: Oil made from plastic often has leftover double grips that make it less stable. Refiners can add hydrogen like this to calm it down.

intro: Adding hydrogen to ethylene turns it into ethane. Food makers use the same trick to turn liquid oil into solid margarine.
takeaway: Opening a double bond frees up two hands, and those hands can grab new atoms.

name: Making ethylene
dH: about +137 kJ per mole of ethane
story: Ethane is content: every hand is held. To change it, you have to pour in a lot of heat, around 800 °C.
The shaking tears one hydrogen off each carbon. Each carbon now has 1 empty hand.
The 2 loose hydrogens grab each other and leave as hydrogen gas (H2).
The 2 carbons use their empty hands to grab each other a second time: a double bond. That's ethylene. The new set holds on less tightly than the old one, which is why heat had to go in.
everyday: This is the main step in a steam cracker, a giant furnace that makes ethylene. Ethylene is the starting block for most plastic bags and bottles.

lens.nexus: Ethylene is one of the light gases that can show up when plastic is heated at your plant. Here it is made on purpose.

intro: Cracking ethane to make ethylene, the building block of most plastic. This is the main job of a steam cracker, a giant furnace at a chemical plant.
takeaway: Heat goes in, a double bond comes out. That stored energy is what makes ethylene so useful for building plastic.

name: Cracking a chain
story: Butane is a chain of 4 carbons. Strong heat shakes it until the grip in the middle snaps.
Now there are two 2-carbon pieces, and each has an empty hand where the chain broke.
One piece steals a hydrogen from the other. With every hand held, it becomes ethane.
The piece that lost a hydrogen now has 2 carbons with an empty hand each. They grab each other a second time. That's ethylene.
everyday: Refineries crack long, heavy molecules into shorter ones like this to make more gasoline and gases.

lens.nexus: This is a tiny version of what heat does to plastic at your plant. Long chains snap into shorter pieces. Some pieces get extra hydrogen, and some end up with double grips.

intro: Breaking a 4-carbon chain (butane) into two shorter pieces. Refineries do this all day to turn heavy oil into gasoline and gases. Pyrolysis at Nexus works on the same idea.
takeaway: Heat snaps long chains into short ones. Some of the pieces end up with double bonds, and that's where the useful gases come from.

name: Making polyethylene
energy: gives off heat (needs a catalyst to start)
story: Each ethylene holds its 2 carbons with a double handshake. A catalyst (a helper that isn't used up) gets the first one to let go of its second handshake.
That carbon now has an empty hand, so it reaches out and grabs the next ethylene.
That ethylene lets go of its own second handshake, which leaves a new empty hand at the far end. That hand grabs the next one, and it keeps going like a zipper.
Three ethylenes become one 6-carbon slice. A real chain repeats this thousands of times. Single grips are more settled than double ones, so heat comes out.
everyday: Grocery bags, milk jugs, and squeeze bottles are polyethylene, the most common plastic.

lens.nexus: Your plant runs the story backwards. Heat snaps these long chains apart again, into shorter pieces that make up oil and gas.

intro: Linking ethylenes into a long chain: polyethylene, the plastic in grocery bags and milk jugs. "Poly" means "many."
takeaway: Plastic is the same small piece linked over and over. The double bond is the hook that makes the linking possible.

name: Welding torch flame
energy: gives off heat (needs a flame to start)
dH: about −1,301 kJ per mole of acetylene
story: In acetylene, the 2 carbons hold each other with 3 handshakes at once. That triple bond is packed with energy, like a tightly wound spring.
The flame shakes it apart. The triple bond and the carbon-hydrogen bonds let go, and the oxygen pairs (O2) split too.
Each carbon grabs 2 oxygens and holds each with 2 hands. That's carbon dioxide (CO2), and 4 carbons make 4 of them.
The 4 hydrogens pair up with 2 oxygens to make 2 waters. So much energy comes out at once that the flame can melt metal.
everyday: Oxy-acetylene torches used for welding and cutting metal.
intro: Acetylene burning in a welding torch. It's the hottest common flame, over 3,000 °C, which is hot enough to cut steel.
takeaway: The more energy is packed into the starting bonds, the hotter the flame. Triple bonds pack the most.

name: Making hydrogen from gas
energy: needs heat (about 800-900 °C with a nickel catalyst)
dH: about +206 kJ per mole of methane
story: Methane and steam are both content, with every hand held. A hot nickel catalyst (a helper that isn't used up) and lots of heat, about 850 °C, pull them apart.
Carbon lets go of its 4 hydrogens, and water's oxygen lets go of its 2.
Carbon and oxygen grab each other tightly. That's carbon monoxide (CO).
The 6 loose hydrogens pair up into 3 hydrogen gas molecules (H2). The new set holds on less tightly than the old one, so heat has to keep going in.
everyday: Most of the hydrogen made today starts this way. Much of it goes into making ammonia for fertilizer.

lens.nexus: A good example of a 'needs heat' step. Like pyrolysis, it only runs while you keep paying for heat.

intro: Making hydrogen out of natural gas and steam. Most of the world's hydrogen is made this way, and most of that goes into fertilizer.
takeaway: You can pull hydrogen out of methane, but you pay for it with heat.

name: Making ammonia
energy: gives off heat (needs an iron catalyst, heat, and high pressure)
dH: about −92 kJ per mole of nitrogen
story: Nitrogen gas (N2) holds its two atoms with 3 handshakes, one of the toughest grips in chemistry. That's why the nitrogen in air is so hard to use.
An iron catalyst (a helper that isn't used up) grabs the nitrogens and loosens them. It takes about 450 °C and about 200 times normal air pressure.
The hydrogen pairs (H2) let go too. Each nitrogen now has 3 empty hands.
Each nitrogen grabs 3 hydrogens. That's ammonia (NH3). A little heat comes out, but without the catalyst it would almost never start.
everyday: This is how fertilizer nitrogen is made. Much of the world's food is grown with ammonia from this process.
intro: Making ammonia from the nitrogen in air. Ammonia becomes fertilizer, and about half the world's food depends on it.
takeaway: Some reactions give off energy but still won't start on their own. A catalyst gets them over the hump.

name: Making methane from CO2
energy: gives off heat (needs a warm nickel catalyst, about 300-400 °C)
dH: about −165 kJ per mole of CO2
story: A warm nickel catalyst (a helper that isn't used up) loosens the CO2. Carbon lets go of both oxygens, which frees all 4 of its hands.
The 4 hydrogen pairs (H2) split too, which gives 8 loose hydrogens.
Carbon grabs 4 hydrogens, one in each hand. That's methane (CH4), which is rocket fuel.
Each of the 2 oxygens grabs 2 of the leftover hydrogens. That's 2 waters, and some heat comes out.
everyday: The International Space Station uses this reaction to turn the CO2 astronauts breathe out back into water.

lens.rocket: The plan for refueling Starship on Mars. Pull CO2 from the Martian air, add hydrogen from Martian water, and make methane. Splitting the water also gives the oxygen.

intro: Turning carbon dioxide and hydrogen into methane and water. The Space Station uses it to get water back, and SpaceX plans to use it on Mars to make Starship's fuel.
takeaway: Run burning in reverse, with hydrogen supplying the energy, and you get fuel back from CO2.

name: Fuels that light on touch
energy: gives off heat (lights on contact, no spark needed)
story: Hydrazine and nitrogen tetroxide are both uneasy, unstable molecules. The moment they touch, they start tearing each other apart.
The weak nitrogen-to-nitrogen and nitrogen-to-oxygen grips break, and hydrazine loses its hydrogens.
Nitrogens find each other and hold on with 3 handshakes each. That's nitrogen gas (N2), one of the most settled molecules there is.
The hydrogens and oxygens team up as water. Going from uneasy to very settled releases a huge burst of heat all at once.
everyday: Satellites and space probes use hydrazine-type fuels for small steering thrusters, because the fuels stay liquid for years without cooling.

lens.rocket: The Apollo lunar module burned a hydrazine mix with nitrogen tetroxide. SpaceX's Dragon thrusters use a close cousin, MMH, with the same oxidizer. These fuels are very toxic.

intro: Two rocket fuels that catch fire the instant they touch, with no spark needed. Spacecraft thrusters use them because they work reliably for years.
takeaway: The bigger the drop from unstable to settled, the more energy comes out. Here the drop is big enough that it lights itself.

name: Photosynthesis
dH: about +2,803 kJ per mole of glucose
story: This is burning in reverse, so energy has to go in. The plant catches it from sunlight.
Light energy pulls water apart. The plant saves the hydrogens. The oxygens pair up and drift away as oxygen gas (O2), the air you breathe.
The plant takes in CO2 one molecule at a time and uses the saved hydrogens to rework it. Six carbons get linked together, and five of them plus one oxygen close into a ring.
Hydrogens and oxygen-hydrogen pieces fill the remaining hands. The result is glucose, a sugar that holds the sunlight's energy in its bonds.
everyday: Every leaf does this. When you eat, your body runs it in reverse to get that stored energy back, breathing out CO2 and water.
intro: How plants make sugar from air and water, using sunlight. It's burning run backwards, and it's where the energy in your food comes from.
takeaway: Plants store sunlight as bonds. When you eat, your body burns those bonds back into CO2 and water.
